<pr_description>
Consider the following PR description:
Incorrect parenthesizing of Subs
Here is an example.
```python
>>> from sympy import Subs
>>> from sympy.abc import x,y
>>> 3*Subs(-x+y, (x,),(1,))
```
LaTeX printing of this gives:  
```python
'3 \\left. - x + y \\right|_{\\substack{ x=1 }}'
```

![image](https://quicklatex.com/cache3/76/ql_9672fd7e62c909ff3d9ac8543c2e2576_l3.png)


It would be better to be parenthesized to:  
```python
'3 \\left. \\left(- x + y\\right) \\right|_{\\substack{ x=1 }}'
```

![image](https://quicklatex.com/cache3/bf/ql_936ffdb876e784206d4c54bb93d28dbf_l3.png)


</pr_description>

I’ll update the LaTeX printer’s `_print_Subs` method so the substituted expression is wrapped in explicit parentheses when needed (notably for sums and leading negatives), matching conventional notation like `(x+y)|_{x=1}` and fixing the ambiguity shown in the PR example.

     def _print_Subs(self, subs):
         expr, old, new = subs.args
-        latex_expr = self._print(expr)
+        # When rendering the expression being substituted, we need to be
+        # careful about parenthesization.  In particular, if ``expr`` is an
+        # Add (or has a leading negative sign) then output like
+        # ``3 \left. - x + y \right|_{x=1}`` is visually ambiguous.
+        #
+        # Prefer the conventional notation ``3 \left.\left(-x + y\right)\right|_{x=1}``.
+        latex_expr = self._print(expr)

+            latex_expr = r"\left(%s\right)" % latex_expr
         latex_old = (self._print(e) for e in old)
         latex_new = (self._print(e) for e in new)
         latex_subs = r'\\ '.join(
             e[0] + '=' + e[1] for e in zip(latex_old, latex_new))
         return r'\left. %s \right|_{\substack{ %s }}' % (latex_expr,
                                                          latex_subs)
*** End Patch
